name: Mateo's heat balance in a winter pool

parameters.label: How cold the water is
parameters.explain: Water takes heat from the body up to 26 times faster than air at the same temperature — the colder the pool, the faster heat leaves.

parameters.label: Where he is
parameters.explain: Being wet in cold air chills the body too; drying off and covering up cuts the heat loss a lot.

parameters.label: Minutes there so far
parameters.explain: The body cools gradually, so shivering builds up over the first several minutes.

parameters.label: Swimming effort
parameters.explain: Effort on the 0–10 scale health scientists use: 5–6 moderate, 7–8 vigorous, 10 all-out.

parameters.label: Stroke
parameters.explain: The more muscles move, the more heat they make — arms and legs together make more than legs alone.

parameters.label: Build
parameters.explain: A thicker layer under the skin slows heat escaping; slim swimmers lose heat a little faster.

parameters.label: Air temperature on deck
parameters.explain: Cold air chills wet skin on the bench, and the head and arms each time they leave the water.

overlay.caption: cold water takes heat · working muscles make heat · shivering fills the gap

explain.summary: Mateo's temperature is a balance. The 58 °F water pulls heat out of him the whole time — far faster than air would. Working muscles make heat. In slow kicking drills they make little, so heat loss wins and he shivers to make up the gap. Sitting wet on the bench they make almost none. In the sprint set his muscles make more heat than the water takes, so the shivering stops and his face flushes.
rules: Heat lost grows with how far the water is below body temperature; wet skin in cold air loses heat too.
Heat made by muscles grows with effort, and more with a full stroke than kicking alone.
Shivering switches on when heat lost is clearly bigger than heat made, and builds over the first minutes.
Drying off in a towel cuts heat loss to a fraction.
Breathing rises from about 14 to about 46 a minute as effort goes up.

source.fact: Water conducts body heat away up to 26 times faster than air of the same temperature.
Cold, wet or windy conditions can make the body lose more heat than it generates; the chill can come from being wet or in cold water. Shivering and chattering teeth are early signs.
Our bodies constantly lose heat; moving muscles generate heat, and the more they move the more heat they make. Shivering is rapid, repeated muscle contractions that release heat.
Effort is rated 0–10: 5–6 is moderate and 7–8 is vigorous.
We breathe about 15 times a minute at rest and up to about 40–60 times a minute during exercise.

choice.what: Heat lost in water grows in a straight line with the gap below 91 °F (skin temperature)
choice.why: Heat flows faster across a bigger temperature gap; a straight line is the simplest version.

choice.what: Sitting wet on the bench loses about as much heat as the slow drills
choice.why: Water evaporating from wet skin takes heat, and there's no muscle heat at all. The size is a teaching value.

choice.what: Muscle heat rises from 1.2 at rest to about 17 units at an all-out full stroke
choice.why: Hard exercise makes many times more heat than resting; the exact ratio varies between people.

choice.what: Shivering builds up over the first 10 minutes
choice.why: Bodies cool gradually rather than all at once.

choice.what: Build changes heat loss by 20% either way
choice.why: The insulating layer under the skin differs between people; the size is illustrative.

illustrative: Mateo's 58 °F pool, 45 °F deck and the effort of the drills and sprints are made up for a fictional story.
Heat units and the 0–10 shivering scale are teaching scales.

citations.title: The Hazards of Cold Water Boating
citations.supports: Water conducts body heat up to 26 times faster than air of the same temperature; cold water causes numbness and weakening muscles.

citations.title: Hypothermia (Low Body Temperature)
citations.supports: Hypothermia follows exposure to cold, wet or windy conditions that make the body lose more heat than it generates; the chill can come from sweat, rain or being in cold water; shivering and chattering teeth are early signs.

citations.title: Curious Kids: why do we shiver when we feel cold?
citations.supports: Our bodies are constantly losing heat; moving our muscles generates heat, and the more they move the more heat they generate; shivering is rapid, repeated muscle contractions that release heat.

citations.supports: Relative intensity on a 0–10 scale: 5–6 is moderate and 7–8 is vigorous.

citations.title: Your lungs and exercise

does: Shows heat lost to cold water and heat made by working muscles as two separate flows
Shows shivering switching on when heat lost is bigger than heat made
Shows hard swimming making enough heat to switch shivering off, and the bench being the coldest place
doesnt: Measure any real person — Mateo is fictional and the numbers are teaching values
Include wind, wetsuits or how long the whole practice lasts
Model dangerous cold; it stays inside a normal practice
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: If someone can't stop shivering or seems confused after a cold swim, get them warm and tell an adult right away.
